html:
The Celts were the Iron Age peoples of Europe who spoke Celtic languages, from Ireland and Iberia to Anatolia. The map shows the label from 400 to 100 BCE, when Celtic peoples held much of central and western Europe. The chart's bar is Celtic Europe.

Their culture is traced through the Hallstatt culture of central Europe, about 800 to 450 BCE, and the La Tène culture after it, with its swirling art in metal. They were never one nation but many tribes: Gauls, Britons, the Celtiberians, the Boii and others, ruled by warrior nobles with druids as priests and judges. They built large hillforts and later towns the Romans called oppida, and made fine iron weapons and gold neck rings, or torcs.

In the 300s BCE Celtic bands moved south and east:

  • around 390 BCE a Gallic army beat Rome at the Allia and sacked the city;
  • in 279 BCE others attacked Delphi in Greece;
  • some crossed to Anatolia and settled Galatia.

Rome then pushed back. It conquered northern Italy and Iberia, and Caesar took Gaul in the 50s BCE, as he tells in his Gallic War. Celtic languages survived in Britain, Ireland and Brittany, and live on in Irish, Welsh, Scottish Gaelic and Breton.
